topics.name: The Mole and Stoichiometry
topics.summary: Counting particles by weighing: the mole, molar mass, and calculating how much product a reaction gives.

lessons.title: The Mole: Counting Atoms by Weighing

objectives.text: Define the mole and state Avogadro’s constant.
Convert between mass, moles and number of particles.
Calculate molar mass from a chemical formula.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
6.02 × 10²³ — the number of particles in one mole.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
The mass of an atom relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Chemical reactions happen between individual particles, but no one can count particles. The mole is the bridge: it converts a mass you can weigh into a number of particles you can reason about.

sections.heading: Why chemists need the mole
sections.body:
An equation like 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is a statement about COUNTS: two hydrogen molecules for every one oxygen molecule.

But you cannot count molecules in a laboratory. You can only weigh things. And weighing equal masses does not give equal counts, because atoms have different masses — 1 g of hydrogen contains far more atoms than 1 g of lead.

The mole solves this. It is simply a counting unit for very large numbers, the way "a dozen" is a counting unit for twelve.

    1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles

That number, Avogadro’s constant, is enormous because atoms are tiny. One mole of water is about a mouthful.

sections.heading: Molar mass
sections.body:
Here is the elegant part. The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams, equals its relative atomic or formula mass.

    Carbon:  relative atomic mass 12  →  1 mol weighs 12 g
    Water:   relative formula mass 18  →  1 mol weighs 18 g

To find the relative formula mass, add up the atomic masses in the formula:

    H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18
    CO₂ = 12 + (2 × 16) = 44
    CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100

So weighing out 100 g of calcium carbonate gives you exactly one mole of it — 6.02 × 10²³ formula units — without counting anything.

sections.heading: The key equation
sections.body:
Everything in this topic rests on one relationship:

    moles = mass (g) / molar mass (g/mol)

Rearranged as needed:

    mass = moles × molar mass
    molar mass = mass / moles

And to reach particles:

    number of particles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³

A reliable habit: write down what you are given, what you want, and which equation connects them, BEFORE substituting numbers.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Calculate the number of moles in 25 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, and how many formula units that is.
sections.example:
Step 1 — Molar mass of CaCO₃:
    Ca = 40
    C  = 12
    O₃ = 3 × 16 = 48
    Total = 100 g/mol

Step 2 — Moles:
    moles = mass / molar mass
          = 25 / 100
          = 0.25 mol

Step 3 — Particles:
    = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³
    = 1.505 × 10²³ formula units

Sanity check: 25 g is a quarter of 100 g, so 0.25 mol. If your answer had come out greater than 1 mol, something went wrong.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. How many moles are in 36 g of water (H₂O)?
2. What is the mass of 2 moles of CO₂?
3. How many atoms are in 0.5 mol of sodium?
4. 4.4 g of a gas turns out to be 0.1 mol. What is its molar mass — and can you name the gas?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
• Molar mass in g/mol equals relative formula mass — add the atomic masses.
• moles = mass / molar mass, rearranged as required.
• particles = moles × 6.02 × 10²³.
• Always sanity-check the size of your answer against the molar mass.

objectives.text: Explain why atoms form bonds at all.
Describe ionic bonding as transfer and covalent as sharing.
Link bonding type to melting point, conductivity and solubility.

keyTerms.definition: An atom that has gained or lost electrons and so carries a charge.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A regular repeating 3-D arrangement of ions.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Why atoms bond, the two main ways they do it, and how the bonding explains properties you can observe — why salt melts at 801°C but candle wax melts in your hand.

sections.heading: Why atoms bond
sections.body:
Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell of electrons, which is a more stable, lower-energy arrangement.

The noble gases already have full outer shells, which is precisely why they are famously unreactive. Every other element achieves the same thing by losing, gaining or sharing electrons.

That gives two routes:
• Metal + non-metal → electrons are TRANSFERRED → ionic bonding
• Non-metal + non-metal → electrons are SHARED → covalent bonding

sections.heading: Ionic bonding
sections.body:
A metal atom loses its outer electrons; a non-metal gains them. Both end up with full shells, and both are now charged.

Sodium chloride:
    Na has 1 outer electron → loses it → Na⁺
    Cl has 7 outer electrons → gains 1 → Cl⁻

The opposite charges attract strongly. Crucially, this is not a bond between one Na⁺ and one particular Cl⁻ — each ion attracts every oppositely charged neighbour, building a giant LATTICE extending in all directions.

That structure explains the properties:
• HIGH MELTING POINT — melting means overcoming attractions throughout the whole lattice.
• CONDUCTS ONLY WHEN MOLTEN OR DISSOLVED — charged ions must be free to move. In a solid they are locked in place, so solid salt does not conduct.
• BRITTLE — knock the lattice out of alignment and like charges meet, forcing it apart.

sections.heading: Covalent bonding
sections.body:
Two non-metals cannot both gain electrons, so they share instead. A shared PAIR of electrons counts towards the full shell of both atoms.

    H₂  — one shared pair (single bond)
    O₂  — two shared pairs (double bond)
    H₂O — oxygen shares with two hydrogens

The shared pair itself is a strong bond. But most covalent substances exist as small separate MOLECULES, and the forces BETWEEN those molecules are weak.

This distinction is the most misunderstood point in the topic. When water boils, you are not breaking O–H bonds — you are separating whole water molecules from one another. The bonds inside survive, which is why steam is still H₂O.

Hence: low melting and boiling points, and no conductivity, because there are no free charged particles.
sections.example:
Why does sodium chloride melt at 801°C while chlorine gas boils at −34°C, when both involve chlorine?

NaCl — a giant ionic lattice. Melting requires breaking strong attractions between millions of ions. Enormous energy.

Cl₂ — small molecules. The Cl–Cl covalent bond is strong, but boiling only has to separate molecules from each other, and the forces between them are weak. Very little energy.

The lesson: melting and boiling points tell you about the forces BETWEEN particles, not the bonds within them.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Magnesium oxide (MgO) melts at 2852°C. What bonding does it have, and why is its melting point even higher than NaCl’s?
2. Explain why solid NaCl does not conduct electricity but molten NaCl does.
3. Predict the bonding in CH₄ and give two expected properties.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Atoms bond to achieve full outer shells.
• Metal + non-metal → transfer → ions → giant lattice.
• Non-metal + non-metal → sharing → covalent bonds → usually small molecules.
• Ionic: high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved, brittle.
• Covalent molecular: low melting point, does not conduct.
• Melting point reflects forces BETWEEN particles, not bond strength within them.

questions.question: How many particles are in one mole of a substance?
questions.explanation: One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles — Avogadro’s constant. It is a counting unit for very large numbers, in the same way a dozen is a counting unit for twelve.

questions.question: What is the molar mass of CO₂?  (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Add the atomic masses in the formula: carbon contributes 12, and there are two oxygens contributing 2 × 16 = 32. So 12 + 32 = 44 g/mol. Choosing 28 means only one oxygen was counted.

questions.question: How many moles are in 36 g of water, H₂O?  (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol. Then moles = mass / molar mass = 36 / 18 = 2 mol. A quick sanity check: 36 g is twice 18 g, so 2 moles.

questions.question: A sample of 0.1 mol of a gas has a mass of 4.4 g. What is its molar mass?
questions.explanation: Rearrange the key equation: molar mass = mass / moles = 4.4 / 0.1 = 44 g/mol. Dividing by 0.1 multiplies by 10, which trips people up. A molar mass of 44 g/mol suggests the gas is carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What type of bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal?
questions.explanation: A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion and a non-metal gains them to form a negative ion. The opposite charges attract, which is ionic bonding. Covalent bonding is sharing, and happens between two non-metals.

questions.question: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, while molten sodium chloride does?
options: The ions are destroyed when solid
The ions are fixed in the lattice when solid and free to move when molten
Melting converts the bonding to covalent
questions.explanation: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. The ions exist in both states, but in the solid lattice they are locked in position. Melting frees them, so the liquid conducts. The ions are neither destroyed nor changed — only their mobility changes.

questions.question: When water boils, what is actually broken?
options: The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule
The forces of attraction between separate water molecules
questions.explanation: Boiling separates whole molecules from one another by overcoming the weak forces between them. The strong covalent O–H bonds inside each molecule survive, which is why steam is still H₂O rather than hydrogen and oxygen gas. Melting and boiling points tell you about forces BETWEEN particles, not bonds within them.
